items.stem: At about what age do most children produce their first recognisable words?
items.answer: About 12 months
items.markingKey: The holophrastic stage begins around 12 months.

items.stem: A child says ‘I goed to the park and I sawed a duck’. Explain which stage of development this suggests, referring to features of the utterance.
items.answer: Post-telegraphic: clause coordination and full sentence structure, with virtuous errors (goed, sawed).
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 per valid point: identifies the stage (post-telegraphic); refers to a specific feature (clause coordination and full sentence structure, with virtuous errors (goed, sawed)); gives a typical age range or contrasts with the next stage.

items.stem: A child says ‘no bed’. Explain which stage of development this suggests, referring to features of the utterance.
items.answer: Two-word: negation placed before the word (Bellugi stage 1).
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 per valid point: identifies the stage (two-word); refers to a specific feature (negation placed before the word (Bellugi stage 1)); gives a typical age range or contrasts with the next stage.

items.stem: These are 6 utterances recorded from Kwame, aged about two: ‘he kicked ball’ | ‘want milk’ | ‘birthday cake’ | ‘where ball’ | ‘no bath’ | ‘teddy falled down’. Using Brown’s rules (count each word and each inflection such as plural -s, -ing and regular -ed as a morpheme; compounds, diminutives and irregular past forms count as one), calculate the mean length of utterance (MLU) in morphemes to 2 decimal places.
items.answer: Morphemes: he kicked ball = 4, want milk = 2, birthday cake = 2, where ball = 2, no bath = 2, teddy falled down = 4. Total 16 ÷ 6 = 2.67.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks: correct morpheme counts (e.g. he kick + ed ball = 4; want milk = 2; birthday cake = 2); total 16; MLU 2.67.

items.stem: These are 7 utterances recorded from Priya, aged about two: ‘no bath’ | ‘all gone’ | ‘birthday cake’ | ‘went park’ | ‘grandma comes’ | ‘teddy falled down’ | ‘kitty eating fish’. Using Brown’s rules (count each word and each inflection such as plural -s, -ing and regular -ed as a morpheme; compounds, diminutives and irregular past forms count as one), calculate the mean length of utterance (MLU) in morphemes to 2 decimal places. Then state which of Brown’s stages this MLU suggests.
items.answer: Morphemes: no bath = 2, all gone = 2, birthday cake = 2, went park = 2, grandma comes = 3, teddy falled down = 4, kitty eating fish = 4. Total 19 ÷ 7 = 2.71. This falls in Brown’s Stage III.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks: correct morpheme counts (e.g. no bath = 2; all gone = 2; birthday cake = 2); total 19; MLU 2.71; Stage III.

items.stem: Three utterances were recorded from children of different ages: (i) ‘up’ (ii) ‘[cooing] ooo (.) aah’ (iii) ‘ba ba ba ba’. (a) Identify the stage shown by ‘up’. (b) Give the typical age range for the stage shown by ‘ba ba ba ba’. (c) Explain how ‘ba ba ba ba’ differs from the stage before it.
items.answer: (a) Holophrastic (one-word) (b) 0–12 months (c) Reduplicated (canonical) babbling of consonant–vowel syllables (about 6–8 months).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: holophrastic (one-word) [1] (b) 1 mark [1] (c) 1 mark difference; 2 marks development with reference to the utterance [3]

items.stem: Which theorist is associated with the language acquisition device (LAD)?
items.answer: Noam Chomsky
items.markingKey: Chomsky proposed an innate LAD and universal grammar.

items.stem: Explain how children’s virtuous errors such as ‘mouses’ and ‘runned’ can be used as evidence in the debate about how children acquire language.
items.answer: It challenges behaviourism: adults do not model these forms, so they cannot be imitated.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 per valid point: describes the evidence accurately; links it to a theory (challenges behaviourism); explains why (adults do not model these forms, so they cannot be imitated); notes a limitation of the evidence.

items.stem: Explain one key difference between the nativist and cognitive explanations of child language acquisition.
items.answer: The nativist view stresses an innate capacity, the LAD and universal grammar (Chomsky); the cognitive view stresses language following cognitive development (Piaget).
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: accurate summary of the nativist view; accurate summary of the cognitive view; a clear point of difference, ideally with an example.

items.stem: Read this transcript of Amara and her older brother playing with toy cars; the child is 2 years 8 months. (Key: (.) micropause; CAPITALS = stress; [ ] non-verbal; C = child.) ‘BROTHER: whose car is this C: mine car BROTHER: it’s MY car (.) you’ve got the blue one C: no (.) me want red (.) no blue BROTHER: okay have the red one C: red one go fast (.) brrm BROTHER: why’s it go fast C: cos it big wheels’ Explain how features of this transcript could be used to support or challenge two theories of language acquisition.
items.answer: ‘mine car’ (pronoun error): shows developing pronoun system. ‘no (.) me want red (.) no blue’ (negation with ‘no’ at the front): stage-like development of negation. ‘red one go fast’ (telegraphic utterance): typical telegraphic stage.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 per valid point: ‘mine car’ (pronoun error) – shows developing pronoun system; ‘no (.) me want red (.) no blue’ (negation with ‘no’ at the front) – stage-like development of negation; ‘red one go fast’ (telegraphic utterance) – typical telegraphic stage; ‘brrm’ (onomatopoeia / sound play) – play and imitation; ‘why’s it go fast’ (older sibling’s non-standard input) – input from siblings differs from adult CDS; ‘cos it big wheels’ (copula and possessive verb omission) – emerging subordination with ‘cos’; balanced evaluation of the theories.

items.stem: Read this transcript of Ravi and his mother looking at a picture book; the child is 2 years 3 months. (Key: (.) micropause; CAPITALS = stress; [ ] non-verbal; C = child.) ‘MOTHER: what’s that Ravi C: doggy MOTHER: no (.) that’s a horse (.) a HORSE C: horse (.) big doggy horse MOTHER: yes it’s a big horse (.) what’s the horse doing C: horse eat MOTHER: that’s right (.) the horse is eating grass C: me eat grass [laughs] MOTHER: no (.) you don’t eat grass silly’ Explain how features of this transcript could be used to support or challenge two theories of language acquisition.
items.answer: ‘C: doggy’ (categorical overextension): supports cognitive views: the child is forming categories. ‘big doggy horse’ (telegraphic utterance): typical of the telegraphic stage. ‘horse eat’ (omission of inflection): shows grammar still developing.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘C: doggy’ (categorical overextension) – supports cognitive views: the child is forming categories; ‘big doggy horse’ (telegraphic utterance) – typical of the telegraphic stage; ‘horse eat’ (omission of inflection) – shows grammar still developing; ‘the horse is eating grass’ (expansion (CDS)) – supports interactionist accounts; ‘me eat grass’ (object pronoun for subject) – common pronoun error before case is mastered; ‘a HORSE’ (prosodic stress (CDS)) – scaffolding through emphasis; ‘what’s the horse doing’ (question to prompt a response) – Bruner’s scaffolding; balanced evaluation of the theories.

items.stem: Analyse the features of child-directed speech in these exchanges and explain how each might support the child’s development, with reference to interactionist theory: (1) ‘CHILD: doggy run / MOTHER: yes, the doggy is running’ (2) ‘MOTHER: [high pitch] ooh WHAT’S that ↗’
items.answer: (1) expansion: the adult expands the telegraphic utterance into a full grammatical sentence. (2) exaggerated intonation: high pitch and exaggerated rise attract attention.

Level 5 (11–12): detailed, insightful analysis of a wide range of features in the data, with precise, apt examples; sophisticated understanding of relevant concepts, theories and research, applied critically to the data; Level 4 (8–10): clear, well-developed analysis of a range of features with appropriate examples; secure understanding of relevant concepts and theories, applied to the data; Level 3 (6–7): some analysis of features with examples; some understanding of concepts and theories, not always linked to the data; Level 2 (3–5): limited analysis, often descriptive; some relevant terminology; theories mentioned rather than applied; Level 1 (1–2): little relevant analysis; mainly paraphrase; very limited terminology. Indicative content: ‘we goed’ (virtuous error (overgeneralised -ed)): regular past-tense rule applied to an irregular verb; suggests rule formation (nativist); ‘I digged a hole’ (virtuous error (overgeneralised -ed)): the -ed rule applied to ‘dig’; challenges imitation-based accounts; ‘you dug a hole’ (recast (CDS)): the father models the correct form without correcting explicitly; interactionist support; ‘two mouses (.) no (.) two mices’ (self-repair with overgeneralised plural): the child applies the plural rule, then attempts a double-marked form; shows active hypothesis-testing; ‘two mice (.) they runned away’ (uptake then a new virtuous error): the child imitates ‘mice’ but overgeneralises ‘runned’; imitation explains some forms but not others; ‘they was scared’ (subject–verb agreement error): ‘was’ with a plural subject; may reflect developing grammar or local dialect input; age 3 years 6 months and expected stage; theories (Skinner, Chomsky, Piaget, Bruner, Vygotsky).
